Swainson's hawk, Buteo swainsoni, exhibits a noteworthy pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is reflected in its adult body masses. Field studies across the Great Plains have documented that adult females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 1109 grams [Wwi = 1109 grams], whereas adult males reach a smaller asymptotic mass of 808 grams [Wwi = 808 grams]. This pronounced difference, with females being roughly 37% heavier than males, is characteristic of many raptorial species and is often linked to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The initial wet weight of newly hatched chicks provides a stark contrast to these adult values; hatchlings emerge from the egg at a mere 61 grams [Ww0 = 61 grams]. Once hatched and freed from the egg shell and fluids, the chick itself has a wet weight at birth of 39.4 grams [Wwb = 39.4 grams]. This relatively modest neonatal mass underscores the rapid growth trajectory the nestling must undergo to achieve its substantial adult size during the brief period of parental care.

The timing of developmental milestones in Buteo swainsoni is tightly linked to thermal conditions during incubation and the subsequent nestling period. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] have a documented incubation period, or age at hatching, of approximately 31 days [ab = approximately 31 days]. This duration is consistent with the incubation periods reported for other medium to large Buteo species and ensures the proper development of the altricial embryo. Following hatching, the altricial chick enters a rapid phase of feather growth and motor skill development. Under typical thermal conditions that support active metabolism in nestlings, around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at fledging is recorded as 35 days [tx = 35 days]. This period of 35 days from hatching to first flight represents a critical phase during which the developing chick must accumulate sufficient muscle mass and flight feather length.

Reproductive output in Swainson's hawk is constrained by a slow life-history strategy typical of long-lived raptors. Females typically lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], and within that annual reproductive event, clutch size ranges from 2 to 4 eggs [N_R_i = clutch size ranges from 2 to 4 eggs]. This modest annual fecundity reflects the high degree of parental investment required to rear such large-bodied nestlings to fledging. The age at which a young hawk first attempts to breed is a key life-history trait that balances survival with reproductive opportunity. Under the metabolic conditions typical of active adults, around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at first brood is recorded as 730 days [tR = 730 days]. This two-year delay before first reproduction allows for complete somatic growth and the development of complex hunting skills essential for successful territory acquisition and chick provisioning.

The attainment of reproductive competence occurs earlier than the actual first breeding event, marking a distinct stage in the life cycle. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturity, is reached at an age of 105 days [tp = 105 days] after hatching under standard thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively early maturation of the reproductive system is intriguing, given that first reproduction is deferred until approximately 730 days after hatching. The extended delay between puberty and first reproduction suggests that behavioral and ecological constraints, such as the need to establish a breeding territory and secure a mate, are more limiting than physiological readiness. This decoupling between physiological and ecological maturation is a common feature among species that occupy large, resource-defended home ranges.

The maximum documented lifespan for Buteo swainsoni provides perspective on the species' overall life-history pace. Longevity records from banding studies indicate that individuals can survive for up to 24.9 years [am = up to 24.9 years] in the wild when maintained under typical metabolic conditions around 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This impressive lifespan, approaching a quarter of a century, is consistent with the pattern observed in other large-bodied raptors that invest heavily in each offspring and exhibit delayed breeding. Within this long adult phase, the daily reproductive rate can be inferred from the combination of moderate clutch sizes and an annual breeding frequency. Given a typical clutch of 2 to 4 eggs produced once per year, the annual reproductive output of a pair is modest, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes adult survival and high per-offspring investment over high fecundity.
